## Speed, Acceleration, Energy, and Power {#sec-lay-ch05}

## A Concrete Picture

A car dashboard separates quantities that casual speech blends together.
The speedometer reports how fast the car is moving now.
Acceleration describes how its velocity changes, including a change of direction.
The fuel gauge concerns stored chemical energy, whereas power describes a rate of energy conversion or transfer.
A heavy truck and a bicycle can have the same speed and very different kinetic energies.
These quantities answer different questions even when they rise together.

The same distinction matters in a swing.
Clubhead speed describes one point, while the club's kinetic energy includes motion throughout the club.
Pelvis angular speed alone does not determine pelvis energy, and a slowing pelvis does not identify where energy went.
A large power peak may deliver little work if it is brief or followed by negative power.
Before interpreting a transfer, name the body or collection of bodies, the point whose motion is reported, the time interval, and the observer frame.
In this chapter, velocities are measured in a declared inertial laboratory frame unless a relative velocity is explicitly named.
Changing the direction of coordinate axes in that frame does not change energy; changing to a physically moving observer can.

![Normalized Speed and Kinetic Energy, and the Effect of Mass at a Fixed Translational Speed.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_speed_is_not_energy.svg){#fig-lay-speed-energy width=96% fig-alt="For fixed mass, speed divided by a reference speed grows linearly while kinetic energy divided by its reference value grows quadratically. A second panel compares translating masses in a one-to-three ratio at the same speed."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### The Point, the Body, and the System

Velocity includes direction; speed is its magnitude.
For a rigid club, the velocity of a head point H is

$$\mathbf v_H=\mathbf v_C+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{H/C},$$

Here C is the club's center of mass, $\mathbf v_C$ its velocity, $\boldsymbol\omega$ the club's absolute angular velocity, and $\mathbf r_{H/C}$ the vector from C to H.
Translation and rotation combine as vectors.
A wrist rate multiplied by club length omits motion of the wrist and may also confuse a relative joint rate with the club's absolute angular velocity.
A flexible club requires additional deformation velocities; one rigid-body formula cannot describe every material point exactly.

Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity.
When speed is nonzero, its rate of change is

$$\frac{d|\mathbf v_H|}{dt}
=\frac{\mathbf v_H\cdot\mathbf a_H}{|\mathbf v_H|}.$$

A Cartesian acceleration component may change sign while speed rises; the tangential component in this equation determines the speed change.
Normal acceleration bends the path and is present even at constant speed.
For a particle moving around a fixed circle, an exactly radial force is perpendicular to velocity and has zero instantaneous power.
A force directed along a club toward moving hands need not be perpendicular to the head's laboratory-frame velocity.
Calling it radial does not establish zero work.

For a translating particle of mass $m$, $K=\tfrac12m|\mathbf v|^2$.
For a rigid segment with arbitrary three-dimensional motion,

$$K=\tfrac12m|\mathbf v_C|^2
+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\omega^{\mathsf T}\mathbf I_C\boldsymbol\omega.$$

The inertia tensor $\mathbf I_C$ and angular velocity must be represented in the same axes.
The familiar $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ is the fixed-axis specialization, with $I$ taken about that axis.
For a translating club, adding a rotational term about the moving grip to a center-of-mass translational term is not generally this decomposition; the reference shift needs its accompanying cross-term.
Using center-of-mass translation and center-of-mass rotational inertia avoids that particular double count.

In generalized coordinates for a system with time-independent position maps,

$$K=\tfrac12\dot{\mathbf q}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf M(\mathbf q)\dot{\mathbf q}.$$

Here $\mathbf q$ contains the generalized coordinates, $\dot{\mathbf q}$ their rates, and $\mathbf M(\mathbf q)$ is the symmetric generalized mass matrix.
Configuration-dependent cross-terms describe shared physical motion.
They do not make the energy of a specified rigid segment arbitrary: its center-of-mass and rotational terms still define it in the chosen observer frame.
What can be arbitrary is assigning each generalized coordinate its own independent energy share while distributing the cross-terms by convention.
Prescribed moving supports add explicit time dependence unless their motion is included among the coordinates; then the simple quadratic expression needs additional terms.
The moving-base chapter returns to that distinction.

### What a Speed Increase Costs

Compare equal-mass idealized clubheads moving at 40 and 44 m/s.
The second is 10% faster and has 21% more **translational** kinetic energy because $(44/40)^2=1.21$.
For a 0.20 kg point-mass representation, those energies are 160 and 193.6 J.
The extra 33.6 J is a useful accounting requirement for that model, not a measurement of extra muscular work.
It could reflect different external work, release of stored energy, lower dissipation, or different initial energy.
A full club also has rotational and possibly elastic energy.

Likewise, a 0.20 kg head at 50 m/s has 250 J of translational energy, while a 70 kg golfer's center-of-mass translation at 1 m/s contributes 35 J.
The latter calculation omits all motion relative to the golfer's center of mass.
It therefore does not say that the golfer's entire kinetic energy is 35 J or that the club contains more energy than the body.
Comparisons are useful only when their included motions are explicit.

A point can speed up while its extended body loses kinetic energy.
As a manufactured example, take a uniform 2 m rod of mass 3 kg with center-of-mass planar inertia 1 kg m$^2$.
At one instant let its center move at $(1,0)$ m/s with acceleration $(-3,0)$ m/s$^2$, its angular velocity be 2 rad/s, and its angular acceleration be 4 rad/s$^2$.
For the endpoint 1 m below the center at that instant, rigid-body kinematics gives velocity $(3,0)$ m/s and acceleration $(1,4)$ m/s$^2$.
Its speed increases at 1 m/s$^2$, but the rod's kinetic-energy rate is $3(1)(-3)+1(2)(4)=-1$ W.
The center's translational energy falls faster than rotational energy rises.
This is a consistent instantaneous mechanics example, not measured golf behavior.
For a single particle, by contrast, increasing speed at fixed mass requires positive **net** power $m\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a$.
Changing coordinates cannot evade that identity.

### Power Needs a Named Interaction

Power is work per unit time.
A force acting at a material point supplies $P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$ using that point's velocity.
For a rigid body, a resultant force and moment represented at C supply

$$P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_C+\mathbf M_C\cdot\boldsymbol\omega.$$

Moment and point velocity must be shifted together if another rigid-body reference is used.
For several deforming contacts, retain their separate force–velocity and moment–angular-velocity pairings unless a common rigid motion has been justified.
One interaction's positive power does not require positive net power after all other interactions are included.
Nor does power at an external boundary always equal total mechanical-energy rate: internal elastic storage, dissipation and, for a biological system, chemical-to-mechanical conversion must be accounted for.

A constant 1,000 W input for 0.05 s supplies 50 J.
A 5,000 W input for 0.002 s supplies 10 J.
For a variable signal the work is its signed integral, $W=\int P\,dt$.
Peak height alone supplies neither that integral nor its sign.
Positive and negative portions can nearly cancel even when both peaks are large.

### Joint Actuator Power and Segment Power

Torque sign is a direction statement, not an energy verdict.
In a planar model, a moment $\tau$ acting on a segment contributes $\tau\omega$ using that segment's absolute angular velocity in the declared frame.
If $\tau$ is instead the actuator moment conjugate to a **relative** joint angle $q$, its actuator power is $\tau\dot q$ using relative angular velocity.
These are different quantities.
In three dimensions, Euler-angle rates are not generally angular-velocity components; their generalized moments must be transformed to preserve power.

For an ideal joint joining two bodies, an actuator applies equal and opposite moments.
If the distal and proximal angular velocities are $\omega_d$ and $\omega_p$, their moment powers are $\tau\omega_d$ and $-\tau\omega_p$.
Their sum is actuator power $\tau(\omega_d-\omega_p)$.
For example, $\tau=2$ N m, $\omega_d=1$ rad/s and $\omega_p=3$ rad/s give moment-power contributions of +2 W on the distal body and -6 W on the proximal body.
Of the 6 W removed from the proximal body through this moment channel, 2 W enters the distal body and 4 W is absorbed by the actuator.
This example isolates the moment channel; any joint-force power must be included separately when finding the total power on either segment.
This does not imply anything about muscle activation or metabolic cost.
It shows why a joint-power label needs its velocity convention.

For a negative moment acting along a declared swing-plane normal, the sign of its contribution also depends on angular velocity along that normal.
Even when that moment channel removes energy from the club, hand forces or other channels can supply more energy than it removes.
Do not add “wrist power” to already complete hand-wrench power if both represent the same transmitted moment.
The final speed depends on the coupled trajectory, rather than the sign of one moment channel.

### A Worked Whole-Club Ledger

Choose the **whole flexible club**, including its shaft, as the system.
Write its mechanical storage as $E=K+V+U_s$, where $V$ includes gravitational potential and $U_s$ is shaft strain energy.
Assume no internal actuator, no shaft damping, and no other omitted work channels for this illustration.
Then

$$\Delta(K+V+U_s)=W_{\rm hands}+W_{\rm aero}.$$

Gravity is represented through $V$ and must not also be added as gravitational work on the right.
Shaft release changes internal storage; it is not another external supply.
Real calculations must add their actual losses and other interactions instead of inheriting these illustrative exclusions.

Consider two intervals of 0.05 s.
In the first, total hand-wrench power averages 800 W, supplying 40 J.
In the second it peaks at 1,500 W but averages only 300 W, supplying 15 J.
Let aerodynamic work be -2 J in each, and let shaft strain energy remain unchanged in the first interval but fall by 8 J in the second.
The ledgers are:

| Quantity | First Interval | Second Interval |
|---|---:|---:|
| Hand work | 40 J | 15 J |
| Aerodynamic work | -2 J | -2 J |
| Change in shaft strain energy | 0 J | -8 J |
| Change in total club mechanical energy | 38 J | 13 J |
| Change in club $K+V$ | 38 J | 21 J |

The second whole-club energy gain is **13 joules**, while its $K+V$ gain is 21 J because strain energy decreases.
Adding the 8 J to the whole-club gain would count an internal conversion as new energy.
If instead the system is just a rigid head, excluding the shaft, shaft-to-head interface work is external to that subsystem.
To split the second interval consistently, add two illustrative assumptions: the shaft's own $K+V$ rises by 5 J, and all -2 J of aerodynamic work acts on the head.
The shaft's mechanical-energy change is then $5-8=-3$ J, so 15 J entering from the hands and 18 J leaving through the head interface close its ledger.
The head receives those 18 J and loses 2 J aerodynamically, gaining 16 J.
The head's 16 J and shaft's -3 J sum to the whole club's 13 J gain.
These assigned storage and drag partitions are not measurements: without them or corresponding observations, whole-club hand work alone does not determine head-interface work.
Adding proximal hand work again to that head ledger would count a transmission path twice.

Equal terminal head speeds therefore do not establish equal work histories or equal total club energy.
The trials may begin with different storage, distribute energy differently among translation, rotation and shaft deformation, or produce different face and path outcomes.
For a specified rigid club, mass and body-frame inertia do not change just because its orientation changes; changing orientation alters projections and the relation between endpoint speed and the rest of its motion.

### Sequence, Acceleration, and Impulse

An ordered sequence of pelvis, trunk, arm and club speed peaks describes coordination.
It does not demonstrate that one energy package passed along those peaks.
A lower angular speed does not alone prove lower segment energy: translation, axis direction and the inertia tensor still matter.
Track the segment's actual energy change, the work through its boundaries, and any storage or conversion within the selected system [@robertson1980; @winter2009].
Ideal joint reactions can transmit power between individual segments while their net power cancels for the combined system.
Zero net work at that larger boundary does not make a force dynamically irrelevant.

For a fixed collection of material bodies, net external force impulse equals the change in total linear momentum in an inertial frame.
Net external angular impulse equals the angular-momentum change about a fixed point in that frame; moving-reference formulas require their appropriate transport terms.
Work instead pairs forces with displacement and moments with angular motion.
A perpendicular force may redirect momentum substantially while doing no instantaneous work.
Momentum, energy and speed therefore need separate graphs.

At a fixed state and fixed contact/constraint mode, suitable equations can split generalized acceleration into named force contributions.
These are not automatically separate physical energy supplies.
Power requires the appropriate force–velocity pairing, and coordinate velocity-bias terms must be interpreted together with the changing mass matrix.
Comparing instantaneous contributions also differs from changing an input and following the resulting trajectory.
The force/work and counterfactual chapters develop those distinctions.

### What the Evidence Supports

**Model Result:** In the pinned double-pendulum timing sweep, selected later-drive schedules produce more delivery speed than early drive or the passive baseline under the stated input bounds and event rules.
A separate coupled uncertainty study reports higher held-out 10th-percentile delivery speed for early restraint than late drive, but worse mean planar face/path error.
These are different model comparisons, not one universal optimum or a demonstration of human preactivation.
The [timing results](proximal_distal_energy_transfer/index.html#sec-results-e1) and [uncertainty/control study](proximal_distal_energy_transfer/index.html#sec-uncertainty-control) specify the respective assumptions and outcomes.

**Human and Methodological Evidence:** Tinmark and colleagues measured pelvis, upper-torso and hand kinematics in 45 skilled golfers, using full and partial shots; their reported peak sequence is kinematic evidence, not a direct measurement of the segment energy route [@tinmark2010].
Robertson and Winter's segment-power study used a sagittal linked-body model and data from two walking participants; it supports an accounting methodology rather than a golf-specific transfer magnitude [@robertson1980].
McPhee's narrative review is a map of golf models and measurement methods, not an additional intervention experiment [@mcphee2022].
Keep those evidence roles distinct when reading a claim about how a golfer generated speed.

### Reader Lab: Diagnose a Misleading Result

Suppose a report favors one strategy because head speed rises more steeply late in the swing and wrist power has a larger peak.
First identify the speed point, observer frame, joint-rate convention, system boundary and integration interval.
Compare initial storage and integrate distinct work channels exactly once.
For a whole-club ledger include strain-energy change inside storage; for a head-only ledger use shaft-to-head work at the boundary.
Check the closure residual against the size of the proposed effect, with consistent event detection and numerical resolution.

Then compare the actual task outputs: face orientation, path, impact location, variability and modeled loads.
A speed improvement may be real while “better strategy” remains unsupported.
A large force with little mechanical work may still matter for tissue loading, and mechanical work is not metabolic effort.

Finally, compare schedules from the same admissible state, including controller or actuator memory where the model has it.
Hold parameter choices, event rules and other inputs fixed for that comparison.
If the ranking survives timestep refinement and specified uncertainty tests, it has support within those tested conditions, rather than universal robustness.
If it disappears, investigate numerical error, changed event selection, initial preparation, parameter choices or other altered conditions; disappearance alone does not identify which explanation is responsible.
A simulation intervention does not by itself establish what a human can execute.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The dashboard analogy separates the questions, but the swing couples their answers.
Head velocity combines translation and rotation; joint power depends on relative motion; physical segment energies differ from arbitrary coordinate energy shares.
Changing the system boundary moves an interaction between internal conversion and external transfer without creating or destroying energy.
Those relationships are why apparently contradictory graphs can coexist.

Biological systems also contain chemical energy, active muscle processes and losses that a rigid mechanical model does not resolve.
An internally driven system can increase mechanical energy without positive external wrench work.
Conversely, high muscular effort may coexist with little external mechanical work.
Do not infer muscle action or a coaching prescription merely from a closed rigid-body ledger.

Use “head speed increased,” “club mechanical energy increased,” and “the hands supplied positive work” as separate statements until the accounting connects them.
Avoid “power was stored,” because power is a rate, and “speed was transferred,” because speed is not a conserved substance.
A useful explanation lets readers follow the connection without substituting one quantity for another.
